fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Rudimentary organs vary greatly in development among individuals of the same species, and the degree of reduction of the same organ can differ much between closely allied species; because they are useless, their variations are not checked by natural selection.

fields.label: Work

fields.label: Chapter

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Rudimentary organs in the individuals of the same species are very liable to vary in degree of development and in other respects.

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XIII, “Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs”; section “RUDIMENTARY ORGANS; their origin explained”. Scope: rudimentary organs in animals and plants

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The variance comparison is clear, but suitable open samples exist only for scattered structures and taxa. The causal selection explanation has moderate rather than decisive discrimination.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare within-species variance of rudimentary structures with homologous functional structures, and compare reduction levels among sister species. Elevated variance and divergent reduction support the empirical claim; neutrality tests can assess the proposed release from selection.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Relaxed selection is not the only cause of high variation.

Measurement error rises as structures become very small.

Individual-level samples for vestigial organs are rare.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: A coefficient-of-variation contrast with functional homologues is a direct test of the variability clause. Specimen repositories and matrices contain the raw material for a handful of skeletal cases and do not contain a compiled variability table. Measuring those scans is slow, and measurement error on small parts is a serious but addressable confound.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare coefficients of variation within species, and evolutionary rates among close species, for rudimentary structures versus functional homologues of similar size. The claim is confirmed if rudiments are consistently more variable within species and more divergent among allies, and refuted if their variation matches that of functioning parts after size and measurement error are controlled.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Published samples concentrate on a few famous rudiments, so the result may not extend to rudimentary organs in general.

Small structures have larger relative measurement error, which can imitate high variation.

Age and allometry change the apparent size of a rudiment and have to be separated from individual variability.
